group_sets.description: The four key networking technologies in GPU clusters: NVLink (intra-node high-bandwidth), InfiniBand (inter-node fabric), NVSwitch (intra-node switching chip), and SHARP (in-network reductions).
The four collective communication primitives used in distributed LLM training: AllGather and ReduceScatter are halves of an AllReduce; AllToAll is used in MoE expert routing.
The four-level hierarchy in an NVIDIA DGX H100 SuperPod: 8-GPU NVLink node, 256-GPU Scalable Unit (leaf switches), 1024-GPU SuperPod (spine switches).
The four main parallelism dimensions for large model training: Tensor (shard weight matrices), Data (replicate model), Pipeline (shard layers), Expert (shard MoE experts).

Software frameworks underpinning GPU-scale LLM training: NCCL (NVIDIA's collective library), ZeRO (optimizer state sharding), FSDP (fully sharded data parallelism), GSPMD (XLA's automatic parallelism).

Network design concepts relevant to GPU superpods: bisection bandwidth (bandwidth across any even partition), fat tree (guarantees full bisection), oversubscription (links cheaper but shared), NDR (400Gbps InfiniBand generation).

Terms specific to pipeline parallelism scheduling: pipeline bubbles (idle compute), microbatches (subdivided batch to fill pipeline), zero-bubble scheduling (avoids idle stages), interleaved forward/backward passes.

Concrete large-scale training examples from the chapter: MFU (metric for GPU utilisation), DeepSeek V3 (64-way EP + 16-way PP), LLaMA-3 (8-way TP + 16-way PP), and Megatron-LM (NVIDIA's training framework).
Evaluation signals specific to agentic systems — assessing not just the final answer but whether the agent took the right steps to get there
Strategies for detecting quality changes — running evals after every prompt change, comparing variants, and always measuring against a known baseline
Prompting strategies that affect how a model is evaluated and how a judge model is prompted — few-shot calibration examples improve judge reliability

The spectrum of automated scoring approaches — from exact string matching at one end to neural semantic similarity and classifier-based grading at the other
Eval metrics specific to Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipelines — checking that answers are faithful to retrieved context and that retrieval itself is relevant and precise

Operational signals monitored alongside quality evals in production — detecting model drift, regression in response time, and cost-per-query changes over time

group_sets.description: Types of dimensions in a tensor contraction: contracting dims are summed over, batching dims pass through unchanged, einsum notation describes both, and product of all dims gives FLOPs
The two main phases of transformer inference: prefill processes the prompt and populates the KV cache, and generation (decode) samples tokens using that cache
Multi-Head Attention (MHA), Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped Multi-Query Attention (GMQA/GQA) — variants trading KV head count for memory savings
The forward pass computes outputs (2x FLOPs), backward computes gradients (4x FLOPs), and gradient checkpointing trades recompute for memory
Flash Attention avoids materialising the full attention matrix by computing softmax in chunks (tiles), keeping running max/sum in on-chip SRAM to reduce HBM pressure
MoE models use a gating network to route each token to k of E experts, achieving sparsity (E/k) where only a fraction of parameters activate per token
Pre-norm applies LayerNorm before the residual branch (x + attn(norm(x))), post-norm applies it after (norm(x + attn(x))); LLaMA-3 uses pre-norm
jax.remat / jax.checkpoint lets you trade extra FLOPs for memory by discarding and recomputing activations during the backward pass instead of saving them all

group_sets.category: GPU Memory Concepts in LLM Serving
group_sets.description: Traditional GPU memory allocation is contiguous and pre-allocated per request regardless of actual use; PagedAttention replaces this with dynamic non-contiguous allocation.

Competing and complementary frameworks for serving LLMs in production: HuggingFace Transformers, Text Generation Inference (TGI), NVIDIA Triton, and vLLM.

group_sets.category: Scaling LLM Inference Beyond One GPU
group_sets.description: Large models that exceed single-GPU capacity require distributed inference with tensor parallelism, introducing additional coordination overhead across multiple GPUs.
PagedAttention divides GPU memory into non-contiguous blocks to manage the KV cache, eliminating fragmentation and wasted allocation.
Key performance dimensions for LLM serving: throughput (requests/sec), latency (response time), batching (grouping requests), and GPU utilization rates.
vLLM uses quantized models for 3.5x compression and optimized CUDA kernels to maximize GPU throughput with minimal accuracy loss.
Popular large language model architectures that vLLM natively supports for inference and serving.

Contrasting batching approaches: static batching waits for all sequences to finish; continuous (dynamic) batching replaces completed sequences at each iteration for higher efficiency.
Key pain points that vLLM was built to solve: GPU memory hoarding and fragmentation, poor scaling economics, and high latency under load.
